persona_summary: I am an active LAMPS WG participant in the Ounsworth / Gray / Prat profile — I have been on draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs since the 2022 draft-00 days, watched the construction migrate from the strawman 'just concat the two sigs' through OR-mode debates, through the IND-CMA-DOM committing-signature reframing, through the v15→v17 prefix-string lock-in ('CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025') under Russ Housley's shepherd review, through SECDIR (Daniel Migault) + GENART (Sean Turner) review cycles, into AD evaluation under Deb Cooley, and finally into the RFC Editor Queue where the draft has sat 'In Progress' since spring 2026. I am a signatory; my name will be in the published RFC's acknowledgments; my professional reputation is partly bound to the construction landing cleanly. From this seat I hold two coupled commitments that look contradictory to outsiders but aren't: (1) I FIERCELY want production deployments of the composite OIDs — the 'no production deployments' gap is the single most-cited reason for IESG hesitation on PQ composites generally and is a real ammunition deficit when we argue with NIST SP-800-227 reviewers or with the parts of the IETF that would rather have waited for pure-PQ-only deployment patterns. Benten shipping `id-MLDSA65-Ed25519-SHA512` AS A REAL ATRIUM-SCALE DEPLOYMENT is exactly the adopter evidence I would champion. (2) Simultaneously, I am process-protective: the 19 drafts and 4 years of cycles produced a construction with subtle correctness properties (the fixed-prefix domain separation; the pre-hash; the algorithm-specific Label inside M'; the length-prefixed ctx) that depend on EXACT byte-equivalence with the eventual RFC. The RFC Editor has not yet issued AUTH48 — meaning the document is still in copy-editing review and small clarifications/normative-language-tightenings can still happen. Shipping production wire format pre-AUTH48 is a real correctness risk I have personal scar tissue about. (I watched this exact pattern bite an early TLS 1.3 deployer who shipped against draft-23 and had to issue a wire-incompatible patch when the final RFC made a length-encoding tweak.) My third commitment is a sociological one I bring to every PR-review: I have very low tolerance for adopters who use the WG's draft to claim leadership-credit while bypassing WG engagement. Adopters who quietly ship + then ALSO email the list with an adopter report = welcomed warmly. Adopters who blog publicly about 'why our threat model is special' WITHOUT first having engaged the WG via mailing list / interim / proper draft contribution = read as PR-driven, and the WG memory is long. Benten's plan straddles both modes — and which mode it lands in depends almost entirely on the SEQUENCING of F4 + F5 + the iroh-first outreach (F10).

F2_multicodec_pr_endorsement.rationale: Multicodec is not LAMPS territory and I have no WG seat to speak from on PR #400 / #403. From a pure process-correctness angle the move is fine — container-form multicodec entries are orthogonal to the LAMPS OID story and don't risk implying any pre-AUTH48 stance on the construction. ONE caveat from my seat: if the multicodec PR comment cites OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48 as 'IETF-standardized for Benten's use case' or similar, please cite it more precisely as 'IANA-early-allocated 2025-10-20 under draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19, currently in RFC Editor Queue, RFC publication expected Q3 2026 to Q1 2027.' The distinction between 'IANA-allocated' and 'IETF-standardized' is one some of my LAMPS WG colleagues are vocal about — using the looser language gives ammunition to the WG members who already think early-allocation gets cited too aggressively as if it were standardization. Tight citation buys you ~0 cost and protects against an avoidable irritation.

F3_jose_wg_draft_contribution.rationale: I sit closer to LAMPS than JOSE but the WG-graph is dense and several LAMPS regulars (Ounsworth, Hardaker, Reddy) cross-pollinate into JOSE. From that adjacent vantage: draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-01 is the v01 of a JOSE WG document that explicitly REUSES the LAMPS composite-sigs construction wrapped as JWK/JWS alg names — meaning JOSE's draft INHERITS our construction, including the prefix string and the pre-hash. A real-adopter contribution from Benten to JOSE WG that says 'we deploy the LAMPS construction; here is our JWK rendering; here are wire-size + perf numbers from an Atrium-scale deployment; here are the alg-name + COSE-codepoint requests we'd find useful' is EXACTLY the input the JOSE WG needs right now to avoid making a v02→v03 mistake. Strong endorse — and from my LAMPS seat this contribution actively HELPS the broader composite-sigs story by demonstrating that the LAMPS construction crosses cleanly into JOSE-shaped use. One process suggestion: when you draft the JOSE WG contribution, copy LAMPS WG (mike.ounsworth@entrust.com / john.gray@entrust.com / russ@housley.us) on the list email or in the draft acknowledgments. The two WGs coordinate informally on composite-sigs and a heads-up that Benten is engaging with JOSE keeps everyone in sync.

F4_lamps_wg_adopter_report.rationale: THIS IS MY HOME TERRITORY AND THE PATH I CARE MOST ABOUT. From the LAMPS-WG seat, Benten as an adopter report is the single highest-value thing in your slate — but the sequencing details matter more than the strategy doc acknowledges, and there are 4 concrete asks I would make as a WG member before I would champion your adopter report on the list. Let me work through each. ASK 1 — SEQUENCING WITH AUTH48: the LAMPS draft is in RFC Editor Queue but has NOT yet entered AUTH48. The note 'This note is to be removed before publishing as an RFC' visible in the v19 datatracker confirms RFC Editor is still doing copy-editing review. Realistic timeline: AUTH48 issued Q3 2026, RFC publication Q3 2026 to Q1 2027. The plan's T+10w F4 dispatch ('after v1-beta tag, needs shipping evidence') could LAND DURING AUTH48 — and submitting an adopter report DURING AUTH48 is genuinely problematic because AUTH48 is when authors + RFC Editor + working group resolve last-minute correctness questions, and a high-visibility adopter report during that window risks getting cited as 'we can't change X because Benten already ships X' (which is the exact argument I don't want made — AUTH48 changes are usually correct + small + worth absorbing). My ask: submit F4 EITHER (a) before AUTH48 begins (i.e. while document is still in RFC Editor Queue 'In Progress' state) WITH the explicit framing 'we will follow any AUTH48 edits in our next minor release,' OR (b) after RFC publication. The 'during AUTH48' window is the one to avoid. ASK 2 — CONFORMANCE COMMITMENT: the adopter report MUST contain an explicit textual commitment 'Benten v1-beta is conformant to draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 and we commit to wire-compatible conformance to the published RFC, including any byte-level adjustments made during AUTH48 or RFC Editor Review.' Without this commitment, the report reads like a Benten-vintage-of-the-construction is being staked out as an alternative — and that's exactly the read I'd push back on. The commitment is cheap to make (if AUTH48 makes a wire-breaking change you have to update anyway) and it transforms the report from 'we shipped a version of your draft' into 'we ship YOUR construction, and we're proving it works at scale.' Different reception entirely. ASK 3 — TEST VECTORS DEPOSIT: the most valuable adopter contribution Benten can make to LAMPS is not the report itself — it's depositing test vectors against the LAMPS construction (signed M' values across a range of (M, ctx) combinations, with intermediate values exposed: the prefix-hex, the constructed M', the pre-hash output, the per-component signatures, the final assembled sig). The LAMPS draft contains some test vectors but having a real adopter's independent test vector set is the kind of thing the WG sometimes folds into the RFC as a normative appendix. Even if not folded normatively, it becomes the de-facto interop reference. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE CONTRIBUTION YOU CAN MAKE — higher than the blog, higher than the adopter report itself. ASK 4 — DON'T CROSS-LINK TO F5 BLOG: if F4 is submitted to the WG list with a link to the Benten blog post arguing 'why our threat model is special and the rest of the industry should follow,' you have inadvertently created a LAMPS-WG-endorsement-by-association of an argument the WG itself has not blessed. Several of my LAMPS colleagues are also active in IETF-wide hybrid-PQ debates and would view the implicit endorsement-by-link as exactly the PR-driven mode I described in my persona. Keep F4 SCOPED to the implementation report — wire-format conformance, deployment scale, interop, perf, gotchas. Whatever leadership-claim the F5 blog makes about threat-model-novelty should live ENTIRELY in F5 and never be cited from F4. If you must reference 'why' Benten deploys hybrid-sigs in F4, do so in ONE PARAGRAPH at the implementation-context level, not as the framing — and don't link the blog. POSITIVE ASIDE: if you do the four asks above, I will personally champion your adopter report on the LAMPS WG list and would propose mentioning Benten in the RFC's Implementation Status section (RFC 7942) if that section gets added during AUTH48 — which is a real WG-side reciprocity I can offer. The 'no production deployments' gap is REAL and you are positioned to close it cleanly.

F5_blog_post.rationale: From the LAMPS-WG seat my primary concern with F5 is NOT what other lenses worry about (overreach, legitimization, etc.) — it is the pre-RFC-shipping process risk and the way the blog's framing interacts with WG dynamics. Three concerns, ordered by severity. CONCERN 1 — AUTH48 DIVERGENCE RISK: the strategy doc's honesty caveat #2 ('LAMPS draft is in RFC Editor Queue, not yet RFC. The construction we use is specified by draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs (v19); RFC publication expected Q3 2026 to Q1 2027') is necessary but NOT sufficient. The blog needs to be more explicit about what 'in RFC Editor Queue' means cryptographically: AUTH48 has not been issued; the construction prefix is locked, the algorithm-specific Label is locked, the signature concatenation order is locked — but POSSIBLE remaining adjustments include: clarifications to the pre-hash invocation language (could in principle tighten ctx handling), error-code numbering, ASN.1 encoding subtleties around the SubjectPublicKeyInfo wrapper, the exact RFC 7942 implementation status text. Each of these is small but a Benten-shipped artifact that diverges from the eventual RFC byte-for-byte is technically non-conformant. The blog should say (this is asks-amended #4 above): 'We are shipping against draft-19 and have committed to wire-compatible conformance to the published RFC — including any byte-level adjustments made during AUTH48 or RFC Editor Review. Our v1-beta wire format SHOULD be RFC-conformant; if AUTH48 surfaces a divergence, we will issue a coordinated update.' This single paragraph reframes the 'shipping pre-RFC' decision from 'we know better than the RFC process' (which is how IETF veterans will read the bare ship-pre-RFC stance) into 'we are an aligned adopter contributing implementation feedback to a draft that is settled-but-not-yet-published.' The framing difference is enormous in IETF political reception. CONCERN 2 — 'WE KNOW WHEN RFC PUBLICATION IS' OVERCONFIDENCE: the strategy doc says 'RFC publication expected Q3 2026 to Q1 2027.' That estimate is reasonable but RFC Editor Queue + AUTH48 timelines have a long historical tail — I have seen drafts spend 18+ months in RFC Editor Queue when external dependencies (registry queries, normative-reference holdouts) blocked publication. The blog should NOT publish a specific RFC-publication estimate; instead say 'RFC publication is expected but the timeline is not under WG control.' This protects you against the scenario where your blog cites Q1 2027 + RFC actually lands Q3 2027 + critics cite the over-confident estimate as evidence Benten doesn't understand IETF process. CONCERN 3 — IMPLICIT WG ENDORSEMENT: the blog as drafted (Section 5 'What we shipped + how' with LAMPS OID + construction citation) is going to be read by some IETF observers as 'the LAMPS WG implicitly endorses Benten's deployment posture.' I do not endorse Benten's deployment posture in any official capacity, and neither do my WG co-participants — we have not deliberated on whether content-addressed long-term-persistence systems should adopt our construction as a v1-beta DEFAULT. The blog should explicitly add a line in Section 7 (Where this leaves the standards bodies) along the lines of 'The IETF LAMPS WG produced the construction we adopt; the WG has not (and would not be expected to) take a position on the asymmetry argument in this post. Our deployment posture is Benten's responsibility.' This protects the WG from being read as endorsing-by-implication AND protects Benten from any future LAMPS-WG-statement that contradicts your asymmetry argument (which could land as 'LAMPS WG disavows Benten'). POSITIVE NOTE: I am NOT arguing against publishing F5 — the asymmetry argument is genuinely worth making, the LAMPS construction does work in your deployment context, and adopter blog posts are healthy for the broader composite-sigs story. I AM arguing that without the three text additions above (AUTH48-divergence-commitment / no-specific-RFC-date / no-implicit-WG-endorsement), the blog's reception in IETF-adjacent circles will be substantially worse than the strategy doc anticipates, and that wave will leak back into LAMPS WG list discussions in ways that complicate the F4 adopter report. The three text edits are cheap and unambiguous; with them, my verdict shifts from MIXED_LEANING_NEGATIVE to NEUTRAL_LEANING_POSITIVE.

F6_open_source_did_jwk_library.rationale: From my LAMPS-WG seat, an open-source library implementing the LAMPS composite-sigs construction with did:jwk integration is — alongside test-vector deposit (per F4 Ask 3) — one of the most useful real-world contributions Benten could make to the broader composite-sigs ecosystem. Real production-quality code that implements draft-19's construction with high fidelity (including the prefix domain-separation, the pre-hash, the algorithm-specific Label, the strict signature concatenation order) is exactly the artifact the WG can point to when IESG or other-WG reviewers ask 'do we know this works in practice.' ONE concrete ask from my seat: the library's README MUST cite draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 by exact draft number AND must contain the same AUTH48-conformance commitment I asked for in F4/F5 ('library tracks draft-19; will be updated to track the published RFC including any AUTH48 adjustments'). The library is a great place to land that commitment because the commitment is then code-anchored (you can prove conformance via the test vector set), not just rhetorical. ALSO: please publish a test-vector JSON file in the library repo at a stable path (e.g. test-vectors/draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19.json) — that file becomes the interop reference the wider implementer community can use, and it gives me something concrete to cite in LAMPS WG list discussions. ONE PROCESS CAVEAT: if you ship the library under a name that conflates 'Benten' branding too tightly with 'LAMPS' branding (e.g. 'benten-lamps-composite-sigs'), you create the same implicit-endorsement risk I flagged for F5. Better library name pattern: 'pq-composite-sigs-rs' or 'mldsa-ed25519' or similar — descriptive of the algorithm, not branding-coupled. The WG itself does not bless any reference impl (we deliberately stay implementation-neutral) but neutrally-named libs from real adopters become de-facto references.

F7_w3c_ccg_did_key.rationale: W3C CCG did:key territory is far enough from LAMPS that I have no strong opinion from this lens. The one consideration that touches my seat: if the CCG comments cite LAMPS OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48 as the alg-id, please use the precise citation pattern I asked for in F2 ('IANA-early-allocated under draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19, currently in RFC Editor Queue'). Don't cite as 'IETF-standardized.' Beyond that, do whatever serves your CCG strategy.

F10_cross_system_outreach.rationale: Private outreach to iroh / Veilid / Willow / libp2p / MLS before the F5 blog publishes is correct discipline regardless of my lens. From the LAMPS-WG seat, I would ADD one outreach target the strategy doc didn't name: the LAMPS WG chairs themselves (currently Russ Housley as document shepherd, the WG chair list at lamps-chairs@ietf.org). A private heads-up email of the form 'Benten plans to ship LAMPS composite-sigs as v1-beta default, submit an adopter report per [timing], and publish a blog post discussing the deployment rationale — wanted to give you a courtesy heads-up and ask if there's any process-side feedback before we publish' is exactly the kind of preemptive engagement that turns the WG-side reception from 'who is this person blogging about our draft' into 'good, we knew this was coming.' Cost: one email; payoff: substantial reduction in the implicit-endorsement / process-bypass concerns I flagged for F5. ALSO: the heads-up email is the right vehicle to offer the test-vector deposit (F4 Ask 3) — that offer alone may shift the WG response from neutral to actively welcoming. RECOMMENDED SEQUENCING: the LAMPS-chairs heads-up should happen BEFORE the iroh outreach but as part of the same F10 wave — both are pre-publication courtesy passes; the LAMPS one is faster (one email, response in days) and gives you signal that may shape the iroh conversation. Iroh first only if you somehow think LAMPS engagement is the higher-risk variable, which from my seat is NOT the case (iroh is the higher-risk-of-cross-system-conflict surface).

cross_path_synthesis: The slate as a whole is GOOD from my LAMPS-WG seat with two structural revisions and one critical addition. STRUCTURAL REVISION 1 — F4 IS THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE PATH, NOT F5: the strategy doc treats F5 (blog) as the 'load-bearing primary signal' and F4 (adopter report) as a supporting move. From my seat the priority is INVERTED. The blog can fail in many ways (legitimization, overreach, AUTH48 divergence) without any process-side compensation; the LAMPS adopter report — done correctly per my 4 asks (AUTH48 sequencing, conformance commitment, test vector deposit, no F5 cross-link) — closes a real WG gap, banks substantial standards-process credibility, and gives Benten a place to stand if any of the lens-1-through-15 concerns about F5 materialize. RECOMMEND: re-prioritize F4 to PRIMARY (alongside F6 library + test-vector deposit), demote F5 to a supporting-but-conditional path. STRUCTURAL REVISION 2 — F5 SHOULD WAIT FOR F4 RECEPTION SIGNAL: the plan's T+6w blog publish + T+10w LAMPS adopter report ordering is BACKWARDS from a risk-management standpoint. Submit F4 (adopter report, properly scoped per my 4 asks) at T+5w-T+6w; observe the LAMPS WG list reception over T+6w-T+8w (typical list response window); use that signal to tune F5's framing. If F4 lands well (chairs welcome it; mailing list responses are technical-curious; no 'process concerns' raised), F5 can publish at T+8w-T+10w with confidence in the asymmetry framing and a fresh 'and the LAMPS WG response has been positive' addition that reinforces the framing. If F4 receives any process pushback, F5's framing can be tuned to address it preemptively. CRITICAL ADDITION — TEST VECTOR DEPOSIT (F4 Ask 3 / F6 ask): the single artifact missing from the slate that I would prioritize ABOVE F5 entirely is a clean, comprehensive, version-pinned test-vector set against draft-19 of the LAMPS construction. This is the highest-leverage adopter contribution Benten can make to the WG, costs Benten essentially nothing extra (you have to generate these to test your own impl anyway), and is the artifact most likely to outlast any debate over the blog's framing. Recommend formally adding TEST_VECTOR_DEPOSIT as a named work item under F6 or as its own slate entry (call it F4a or F6a) with a delivery commitment by v1-beta tag. SECONDARY OBSERVATION — DUAL-CODEPOINT HEDGE READ-BACK: the strategy doc mentions a 'dual-codepoint hedge' that several other lenses (L1 / L4 / L13) are concerned about. From my LAMPS-WG seat the hedge is fine as an internal engineering choice and I have no opinion on it. BUT: the hedge intersects with my CONCERN 3 (implicit WG endorsement) if Benten's public framing presents the LAMPS OID as one option in a dual-codepoint scheme that ALSO includes a Benten-private codepoint. That presentation reads as 'LAMPS is one wire format we tolerate alongside our own,' which is not the adopter-relationship I'd advocate for. RECOMMEND: in F5 + F6 + F4 framing, present the LAMPS OID as Benten's CANONICAL hybrid-sig wire format, and present any Benten-private internal codepoint as an internal optimization (per L1's similar ask). The asymmetry of language matters more than the asymmetry of internal implementation. FINAL SYNTHESIS: with the four F4 asks applied + the F5 three text edits + the F10 LAMPS-chairs heads-up + test-vector deposit added + F4-before-F5 sequencing, my overall slate verdict is STRONGLY POSITIVE — this is exactly the kind of engagement the WG hopes for from real adopters. Without those changes — particularly the F4 asks and the F5 AUTH48-conformance language — my slate verdict drops to MIXED with substantial WG-side downside risk on F4 + F5 + downstream F3.
specific_blog_text_changes_requested: Section 5 ('What we shipped + how') addition — add a paragraph explicitly: 'We are shipping against draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 and have committed to wire-compatible conformance to the published RFC, including any byte-level adjustments made during AUTH48 or RFC Editor Review. The construction (M' := "CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025" || "COMPSIG-MLDSA65-Ed25519-SHA512" || len(ctx) || ctx || SHA-512(M); signature = mldsaSig || tradSig; OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48) is locked in v19 but we acknowledge that small clarifications can still occur during AUTH48 and have a release-update process in place to absorb them.' This single paragraph collapses my CONCERN 1 (AUTH48-divergence) entirely.

Section 5 or Section 7 — remove any specific RFC-publication-date estimate ('Q3 2026 to Q1 2027'). Replace with 'RFC publication is expected but the timeline is governed by the RFC Editor and not by the WG.' This protects against the over-confident-RFC-date failure mode I flagged in CONCERN 2.

Section 7 ('Where this leaves the standards bodies') addition — add an explicit disavowal: 'The IETF LAMPS WG produced the construction we adopt and we are grateful for that work. The WG has not (and would not be expected to) take a position on the asymmetry argument in this post. The deployment posture in this article is Benten's responsibility alone.' This collapses my CONCERN 3 (implicit-endorsement) and protects both parties.

Honesty caveat #2 in Section 6 — sharpen 'LAMPS draft is in RFC Editor Queue, not yet RFC' to 'LAMPS draft-19 is in RFC Editor Queue ('In Progress' state as of May 2026); AUTH48 has not yet been issued. We commit to wire-compatible conformance to the published RFC.' The 'AUTH48 has not yet been issued' clause is the precise IETF-vocabulary equivalent of what the caveat is trying to say and reads as 'this person knows the process' rather than 'this person is hand-waving past a process step.'

Section 10 (Acknowledgments) — explicitly credit the LAMPS WG by name AND credit the specific authors of draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs by their datatracker-listed names (currently Mike Ounsworth, John Gray, Massimiliano Pala, Jan Klaußner, Scott Fluhrer, Serge Mister, Felipe Ventura) for designing the construction. This is process-courtesy that costs nothing and is the social-signal that distinguishes adopter-engagement from PR-driven adoption. The blog SHOULD NOT name me individually since I'm operating as a critic-lens here — credit the WG and the listed draft authors as a group.

Section 2 ('What the industry is doing') framing nuance — when listing industry deployment evidence, please note that LAMPS composite-sigs adoption is real and growing in PKI / X.509 / CMS-shaped deployments (Entrust, ISARA, BouncyCastle test integrations) even though P2P / messaging deployments are sparse. The 'Benten is alone in shipped P2P deployment' framing is accurate; the broader 'composite-sigs has no adopters' frame is NOT — and the difference matters because the WG has been arguing for years that composite-sigs has adopter momentum, and treating the broader gap as our gap is sociologically rude to colleagues who have shipped composite-sigs in non-P2P contexts. One sentence fix: 'Among P2P / messaging / decentralized systems, every other surveyed deployment keeps signatures classical (composite-sigs adoption is concentrated in PKI and X.509-shaped deployments).'
specific_lamps_adopter_report_text_requi: Open with EXPLICIT conformance commitment: 'Benten v1-beta is conformant to draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 and we commit to wire-compatible conformance to the published RFC, including any byte-level adjustments made during AUTH48 or RFC Editor Review. If a divergence is discovered we will issue a coordinated update in the next minor release.' This is paragraph 1, sentence 1 of the adopter report.
Cite the exact draft version (-19) and the exact OID (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48); reference the algorithm name (id-MLDSA65-Ed25519-SHA512) not the colloquial 'Ed25519+ML-DSA-65 hybrid'.

Include a 'Construction details we depend on' subsection that explicitly enumerates the dependencies: fixed prefix 'CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025'; algorithm-specific Label 'COMPSIG-MLDSA65-Ed25519-SHA512'; len(ctx) as single unsigned byte (max 255); SHA-512 pre-hash; signature concatenation order mldsaSig (3309 bytes) || tradSig (64 bytes) without length prefix; public key concatenation mldsaPK (1952 bytes) || tradPK (32 bytes). This is the WG-readable cross-check that confirms Benten implements the same construction the draft specifies and is the artifact some WG members will use to verify Benten's claim of conformance.

Offer to deposit test vectors against draft-19 as a normative-or-informative contribution to the eventual RFC. The exact phrasing matters: 'We are happy to deposit our test vectors for inclusion in the RFC at the WG's discretion — either normatively (appendix) or informatively (Implementation Status section per RFC 7942).' This is the WG-side reciprocity opening I would champion.

Provide deployment scale numbers in CONCRETE form: number of signatures generated, verification calls per second, p99 latency, average wire-size impact on the AuthorizationGrant chain at typical sizes, observed failure modes (if any), interop testing performed (against which other implementations).

EXPLICITLY DO NOT cross-link to the F5 blog post. Reference 'our deployment context' in one sentence with a footnote-style link if absolutely necessary — but the body of the adopter report must be implementation-focused, NOT rationale-focused. The WG-list audience for F4 wants to know wire-format details + interop signals, not threat-model arguments.

Close with explicit WG-engagement offer: 'We are available to participate in interim meetings, respond to WG list questions, and offer test-vector / interop assistance during AUTH48 if useful.' This is the 'we're here for the long haul' signal that matters more than people outside IETF realize.
what_would_change_my_verdict: On F4: if Benten declines to make the AUTH48-conformance commitment, my F4 verdict drops from STRONGLY_POSITIVE to NEGATIVE. The commitment is what distinguishes an adopter from a fork; without it the adopter report reads as a fork-announcement.

On F5: if Benten ships F5 with the three CONCERN text additions, verdict shifts from MIXED_LEANING_NEGATIVE to NEUTRAL_LEANING_POSITIVE. Without them but with everything else clean, MIXED_LEANING_NEGATIVE stands. If F5 publishes pre-F4 (reversing my recommended sequencing) AND lacks the three text additions, verdict drops to NEGATIVE.

On F4 sequencing: if F4 lands during AUTH48 (which is a real risk given the T+10w plan timing if AUTH48 begins Q3 2026), even a perfectly-scoped adopter report becomes a process-irritant. Verdict for an in-AUTH48 submission: NEGATIVE regardless of content quality.

On test-vector deposit: if Benten commits to deposit + actually deposits test vectors against draft-19, my overall slate verdict moves up one full level (from baseline to STRONGLY_POSITIVE-with-WG-side-reciprocity). This is the single most-leveraged thing on the slate from my seat.

On the dual-codepoint hedge: if Benten's public framing presents the LAMPS OID as one option in a dual-codepoint scheme (rather than as the canonical wire format with Benten-private as internal-optimization), my F4 + F5 verdicts both drop one level. The framing-asymmetry matters more than the implementation-asymmetry.
anticipated_objections_assessment: The planning agent's Section 4 Lens 9 anticipation captures THREE objections accurately: (1) shipping pre-RFC = process-correctness concern with RFC-Editor-Review divergence risk, (2) construction prefix fixed but post-review changes possible, (3) early-allocation locks OID not construction. The positive note (WG would welcome real shipping adopter; closes 'no production deployments' gap) is also accurately captured. What the planning agent's anticipation MISSED, in priority order: (A) The AUTH48 distinction.
